item.text: {"text":"Repeated perturbations are nested within users; treating every user–permutation result as independent creates pseudoreplication and overstates precision. Hierarchical-bootstrap research recommends respecting the sampling hierarchy, while hierarchical permutation methods restrict exchanges to units justified by the experimental design. For paired model comparisons, compute differences using the same users and perturbations, preserving those pairs during resampling. [Saravanan et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7906290/), [Kulkarni et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9098003/).\n\nApplied recommendation: average paired differences across perturbations within each user, then average users equally; for four-category macro evaluation, resample users within each category and average category means equally. A user-cluster bootstrap preserves each user’s complete repeated-measure block and estimates uncertainty across sampled users. Report finite-permutation Monte Carlo uncertainty separately: with independent perturbation draws across users, its conditional variance is estimated by Σᵢ(sᵢ²/Rᵢ)/U², where sᵢ² is the within-user variance of paired differences. More repetitions reduce this component but do not increase the number of independent users. Resampling both users and repetitions requires care: user means already contain finite-repetition noise, so naïvely adding another resampling layer can double-count it. For hypothesis tests, user-level label swaps/sign flips require exchangeability or symmetry under the null; random history permutations alone do not establish that null. [Monte Carlo error assessment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3337209/), [hierarchical resampling methods](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9098003/)."}
